cue: How do you say someone destroyed the thing that was making them money?

es.text: Matar la gallina de los huevos de oro
es.literal: to kill the hen of the golden eggs
es.meaning: To ruin a reliable source of benefit through greed or short-sightedness.
es.example: Subieron tanto los precios que mataron la gallina de los huevos de oro.
es.exampleTranslation: They raised prices so far that they killed the golden goose.

it.text: Uccidere la gallina dalle uova d'oro
it.literal: to kill the hen of the golden eggs
it.meaning: To ruin a reliable source of benefit through greed or short-sightedness.
it.example: Hanno riempito il festival di sponsor e ucciso la gallina dalle uova d'oro.
it.exampleTranslation: They packed the festival with sponsors and killed the golden goose.

bridge.note: Same Aesop fable, same hen, and both languages agree it is a hen — which is worth saying, because English is the one that wandered off and made it a goose. The crossing is a grammar lesson in miniature. Spanish links the eggs with a plain DE. Italian uses DALLE, from-the, as though the eggs came out of her rather than belonged to her. And that dalle drags along one of Italian's strangest nouns: uovo is masculine in the singular and feminine in the plural, so 'le uova' looks wrong to anyone who has just learned the word.

interference.es_to_it: 'Della gallina di uova d'oro' collapses two things at once. Italian wants dalle uova d'oro — the preposition is da, and uovo goes feminine in the plural, so it is LE uova, not 'i uovi'. The verb also differs: Italian uccidere, where Spanish matar.
interference.it_to_es: Spanish links with a bare de: la gallina DE los huevos de oro. And huevo is regular in Spanish — los huevos, masculine throughout — so the Italian irregularity has nothing to transfer to.
